comparison: Perfect agreement on C5. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers accepted the finding that GREM1 expression does not correlate with fibrosis stage in large public datasets (n=352 patients). This negative correlation finding was not challenged by either evaluation.

Strong agreement on heparin-binding mechanism (C21-C24, C32, C81-C82). Both evaluations praised this as a major contribution. Peer reviewers explicitly noted this 'challenges existing data' on circulating GREM1 detection. OpenEval also includes absence of circulating Gremlin-1 (C19-C20) in R4, while peer review combines these claims together in R4.

Strong agreement on GREM1 upregulation and localization findings (C1-C4, C13-C14). Both accepted the comprehensive characterization using multiple techniques. OpenEval groups more claims together (C1-C14, C77-C78) while peer review separates C15-C16 (protein data) into their evaluation. Both noted the high quality and well-controlled nature of the data.

Agreement on IHC protein findings (C15-C16). OpenEval evaluates these separately, noting consistency with mRNA patterns and potential detection issues. Peer reviewers grouped these with the broader expression characterization (R1) and accepted without challenge.

Partial overlap on cellular localization claims (C6-C12). Both evaluations accepted the heterogeneous and restricted expression patterns. Peer review R3 focuses specifically on RNAscope ISH findings, while OpenEval R1 groups these with broader expression characterization including additional claims.

Agreement on absence of circulating Gremlin-1 (C19-C20). OpenEval R4 focuses on these claims plus C59, while peer review R4 combines these with heparin-binding mechanism. Both noted this contradicts prior literature and represents an important finding.

Agreement on antibody efficacy characterization (C25-C29). Both accepted the demonstration of antibody functionality through multiple assays. OpenEval focuses on these specific efficacy claims, while peer review R5 groups them with broader antibody characterization (C30-C39). One peer reviewer noted minor concern about in-house reagents lacking external validation.

Agreement on detailed antibody properties (C30-C39). Both accepted the characterization of differential antibody properties. OpenEval evaluates these separately from efficacy claims, while peer review groups all antibody characterization together and praised the 'impressive range of in vitro biochemical techniques.'

Strong agreement on negative in vivo findings (C49-C50, C53). Both accepted the lack of therapeutic effect in the MASH mouse model. OpenEval notes adequate study design and confirmed target engagement. Peer reviewers accepted this as a key negative finding with all three reviewers explicitly acknowledging it.

Agreement on target engagement evidence (C51-C52). OpenEval evaluates this separately as important pharmacodynamic validation. Peer review R7 groups these with the broader in vivo study findings. Both recognized this as evidence the antibody engaged its target despite lack of efficacy.

Agreement on negative in vitro findings in human cells (C40, C43-C45). Both accepted the lack of anti-fibrotic effects. OpenEval R8 includes additional claims (C57-C58, C61) about PCLS findings, while peer review R6 focuses on primary cell data and includes overexpression studies (C41-C42, C46-C48).

Agreement on overexpression studies (C41-C42, C46-C48, C79-C80). Both accepted that overexpression changed BMP pathway genes but not fibrogenic markers. OpenEval evaluates these separately as key negative findings, while peer review groups them with other in vitro negative results.

Agreement on PCLS validation and negative findings (C54-C56, C60). Both accepted that the PCLS system was responsive to controls and that antibody penetrated tissue, strengthening the negative findings. OpenEval emphasizes this as validation of the assay system, while peer review R8 also includes the negative PCLS results (C57-C58, C61).

Agreement on negative PCLS findings (C57-C58, C61). Both evaluations accepted the lack of anti-fibrotic effects in human cirrhotic tissue. OpenEval groups these with other human model negative results, while peer review specifically highlighted the use of human ex vivo tissue as a study strength.

Strong agreement on overall conclusions (C76, C83-C84). Both accepted that Gremlin-1 is not a viable therapeutic target for MASH fibrosis. OpenEval notes the conclusion is well-supported by breadth of evidence with appropriate acknowledgment of limitations. Peer reviewers praised the study as 'impressive tour-de-force' and 'critically important' for challenging less rigorous literature.

Minimal overlap on C77-C78 (rat model findings). OpenEval includes these in the comprehensive expression characterization (R1), while peer review R9 groups them with overall conclusions. Both accepted these findings without challenge.

Partial overlap on C79-C80 (overexpression without fibrogenic effect). OpenEval evaluates these as part of in vitro negative findings (R9), while peer review includes them in overall conclusions (R9). Both accepted these as supporting the lack of therapeutic potential.

Minimal overlap on C59 (absence of circulating Gremlin-1 in rats). OpenEval groups this with human circulation data (R4), while peer review includes it with PCLS findings (R8). Both accepted the finding without challenge.

OpenEval identified uncertainty regarding prior literature claims (C17-C18) that conflict with current findings. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these cited claims, though they acknowledged the paper 'challenges existing data' and praised studies that 'challenge less vigorous studies in the literature.'

OpenEval marked extensive background literature claims (C62-C75, C85-C89) as uncertain since they cannot be independently verified. Peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these background citations, focusing instead on the experimental findings and conclusions.
